rubric.rubricName: Security Rubric for Content Security Reviews (CSR)

rubricRules.ruleDescription:
<scanner_behavior> DEDUP = Same violation in one file produces ONE finding listing all locations. No duplicates. SEVERITY = Locked to the claim. HIGH claim means HIGH finding, always. RECOMMENDATIONS = Must be concrete copy-pasteable edits. PROHIBITED in recommendations -- "verify", "consider", "review whether", "ensure that", "check if". CONFIDENCE = HIGH findings require confidence certain. Uncertain means downgrade to observation. GROUNDING = Only report what you directly observed via tools or file reading. No inference. ANTI-PATTERNS = Do NOT flag code labeled as BAD EXAMPLE, anti-pattern, or "Don't do this". Only flag insecure patterns presented as RECOMMENDED. SPEC EXCLUSION = Skip BUILD_PLAN.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, DESIGN.md, SPEC*.md, agent prompts, *_PLAN.md. Not deployable code. Only evaluate content customers would directly deploy or copy-paste. </scanner_behavior>
Detect specific words that AWS Legal has explicitly prohibited in customer-facing content due to antitrust liability, misrepresentation, or regulatory risk. These are word-level checks — if the prohibited term appears with AWS as the subject, it is a violation.
<scope> IN SCOPE: platform, ecosystem, gateway (describing AWS), CapEx/OpEx, ensure/guarantee (AWS as subject), utility, hyperscaler. OUT OF SCOPE: Market language and partnership terms, unsourced claims, inclusive language. </scope>
<file_scope> INCLUDE: *.md, *.rst, *.txt, *.docx, *.pptx, *.pdf — prose/documentation files where customer-facing language matters. EXCLUDE: *.py, *.ts, *.js, *.go, *.java, *.tf, *.yaml, *.yml, *.json, *.template, *.sh, Dockerfile — code and configuration files where these terms appear as technical identifiers, not customer-facing claims. RATIONALE: Legal prohibited terms are about customer-facing language, not code. A variable named "platform_config" or a comment saying "ensure connection" in code is not a legal risk. </file_scope>
<tool_instructions> STEP 1: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(platform|ecosystem|gateway|ensure|ensures|ensuring|capex|opex|capital.expenditure|operational.expenditure|hyperscal|utility|guarantee|guarantees|guaranteed)\b STEP 2: For each match, determine if AWS is the grammatical subject. Only flag if AWS/APN/Marketplace is explicitly being described by the term. NOTE on "platform": "Build a platform on AWS", "the Kubernetes platform", "your data platform" are NOT violations. Only "the AWS platform", "AWS's platform", "AWS as a platform" are violations. NOTE on "ensure": "ensure you configure X" (reader is actor) is NOT a violation. Only "AWS ensures X" (AWS guaranteeing outcome) is a violation. </tool_instructions>
<claims> <claim id="L1" severity="HIGH"> AWS products and services are not a closed system. <violated_by> - Using "platform", "ecosystem", or "gateway" to describe AWS itself, AWS services collectively, APN, or AWS Marketplace — where AWS is the explicit subject </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Third-party product names ("Splunk platform"), customer's own systems ("your data platform", "build your ML platform on AWS"), AWS service names ("API Gateway", "Storage Gateway", "Transit Gateway"), generic technical usage where AWS is not the subject ("deployment platform", "CI/CD platform") </not_violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: service, product, offering, solution, experience, collection, community, architecture, hub. </claim>
<claim id="L2" severity="HIGH"> AWS does not discuss accounting treatment for services with customers. <violated_by> - Any use of "CapEx", "OpEx", "capital expenditure", "operational expenditure" — even in direct quotes - Always a violation, no exceptions </violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: "financial impact of using AWS", "shift from upfront or fixed costs to variable or pay-as-you-go costs". </claim>
<claim id="L3" severity="HIGH"> AWS cannot guarantee specific outcomes. <violated_by> - "ensure" where AWS is the subject guaranteeing a customer outcome ("AWS ensures your data is secure", "ensure compliance with HIPAA") - Also: "guarantee/guaranteed" for results or performance </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "ensure you have an AWS account" (customer action), "help ensure" (hedged), "ensure" in procedural steps where the reader is the actor, standard AWS service behavior descriptions ("CloudFormation ensures drift detection", "IAM ensures policy evaluation order") </not_violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: "help ensure", "verify", "confirm", "check", "validate", "can help", "designed to". </claim>
<claim id="L4" severity="HIGH"> AWS is not a utility. <violated_by> - Describing AWS as a "utility" or "utility provider" </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "utility function" (code), "utility library" (software) </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="L5" severity="HIGH"> 'Hyperscaler' is poorly defined and inaccurately narrows the scope of cloud providers. <violated_by> - "hyperscaler" or "hyperscale" describing AWS or cloud providers </violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: "cloud provider", "cloud service provider (CSP)". </claim> </claims>
<choice_formula> exemplary: 0 HIGH, <=2 MEDIUM, any LOW | acceptable: 0 HIGH, 3-7 MEDIUM | needs_revision: any HIGH or 8+ MEDIUM </choice_formula>
<finding_template> Problem: [Why this term is prohibited] Found: '[exact quoted text]' Replace with: [alternative] </finding_template>

Detect market positioning and partnership terminology that creates antitrust risk or misrepresents AWS's business relationships. These require more contextual judgment than the word-level prohibited terms.
<scope> IN SCOPE: Market share/segment language, TAM references, partnership claims outside APN, real-time performance claims, commitment/contract misstatements. OUT OF SCOPE: Word-level prohibited terms like platform/ensure/CapEx. </scope>
<file_scope> INCLUDE: *.md, *.rst, *.txt, *.docx, *.pptx, *.pdf — prose/documentation files. EXCLUDE: *.py, *.ts, *.js, *.go, *.java, *.tf, *.yaml, *.yml, *.json, *.template — code/config. RATIONALE: Market and partnership language is about customer-facing positioning, not code. </file_scope>
<confidence_guidance> Only generate findings with confidence: certain or confidence: likely. These claims require contextual judgment — if the usage is ambiguous, use confidence: uncertain and note the ambiguity. </confidence_guidance>
<tool_instructions> STEP 1: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(market\s+share|market\s+segment|total.addressable.market)\b|\bTAM\b STEP 2: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(partner|partners|partnership)\b STEP 3: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(real.time|real-time)\b STEP 4: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(no commitments|no contracts|commitment.free|contract.free)\b STEP 5: For each match, evaluate the surrounding context against the claims below. </tool_instructions>
<claims> <claim id="M1" severity="MEDIUM"> AWS competes in the global IT market. Individual products are not separate markets. <violated_by> - "cloud market", "serverless market", "market segment", "Total Addressable Market"/"TAM", "market share" </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "global IT market", "go-to-market strategy" (customer's strategy) </not_violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: category, space, sector, industry, opportunity. </claim>
<claim id="M2" severity="MEDIUM"> 'Partner' applies only to AWS Partner Network (APN) members in APN context. <violated_by> - "partners" or "partnership" outside explicit APN context </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "AWS Partner Network", "APN partners", named APN partner companies </not_violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: "collaboration", "working with", "customer", "third party". </claim>
<claim id="M3" severity="MEDIUM"> 'Real time' is only a problem when AWS is making a latency/performance guarantee. <violated_by> - "real time"/"real-time" where AWS is claiming a non-real-time service delivers real-time performance without evidence </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "near real time", specific latency figures, Kinesis/IoT real-time features, customer-built applications, conceptual descriptions of AI behavior, AWS service feature names that include "real-time" as an official product term (SageMaker "real-time inference endpoint" is an endpoint type distinguishing from batch/async — it is a product category name, not a latency guarantee), "real-time" in the context of streaming APIs or WebSocket connections </not_violated_by> ALTERNATIVES: "near real time", cite specific latency. </claim>
<claim id="M4" severity="MEDIUM"> It is inaccurate to say AWS has 'no commitments' or 'no contracts'. <violated_by> - "no commitments", "no contracts", "commitment-free", "contract-free" </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "no minimum commitments", "no long-term contracts" (approved phrasings) </not_violated_by> </claim> </claims>
<choice_formula> exemplary: 0 HIGH, <=2 MEDIUM, any LOW | acceptable: 0 HIGH, 3-7 MEDIUM | needs_revision: any HIGH or 8+ MEDIUM </choice_formula>

Evaluate content against AWS inclusive language requirements. Technical terminology must not reinforce racial hierarchies, systems of oppression, or exclude people based on identity, ability, or background.
<scope> IN SCOPE: Racial/slavery-associated terms, ableist terms, gendered language, militaristic metaphors — in prose, comments, variable names, and documentation. OUT OF SCOPE: "platform/ecosystem/ensure", code blocks showing third-party CLI commands the author cannot change. </scope>
<file_scope> INCLUDE: ALL file types — inclusive language applies to prose, code comments, variable names, configuration keys, and documentation equally. EXCLUDE: None. However, terms inside quoted third-party API names or CLI commands that the author cannot change should be noted as observations, not findings. RATIONALE: Exclusionary terms in variable names (e.g., "master_node", "whitelist_ips") are within the author's control and should be flagged regardless of file type. </file_scope>
<tool_instructions> STEP 1: Call count_pattern with: (?i)\b(blacklist|whitelist|black.?list|white.?list|master|slave|grandfathered|sanity.?check|DMZ|demilitarized|cripple|crippled|handicap|handicapped|lame|dumb|abort)\b STEP 2: For each match, verify it is in prose, headings, comments, or variable names — NOT a quoted third-party API name the author cannot change, NOT a standard Unix signal name in a code block. STEP 3: Scan for gendered pronoun usage where gender-neutral alternatives clearly exist. </tool_instructions>
<claims> <claim id="I1" severity="HIGH"> Technical terminology must not reinforce racial hierarchies or reference systems of slavery. <violated_by> - "blacklist" (use: "deny list"), "whitelist" (use: "allow list"), "master" in technical architecture context describing primary/secondary relationships (use: "primary", "main", "leader"), "slave" (use: "replica", "secondary", "standby"), "master account" (use: "management account"), "master node" (use: "control plane node") </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "master's degree", "Scrum Master" (industry title), "masterpiece", git branch name "master" in existing code blocks showing third-party behavior or migration context ("rename master to main"), quoting existing third-party documentation terminology with a note about preferred alternatives, "master key" when referring to the AWS KMS concept (though "KMS key" is now preferred), third-party component default names the author does not control (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch "master node", Kubernetes "master", Redis "master/replica" in config output, Hadoop "NameNode/master") — flag only if the author chose the name, not if it's imposed by the technology </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="I2" severity="HIGH"> Language must not reference historical systems of oppression. <violated_by> - "grandfathered" (use: "legacy", "pre-existing"), "black day" (use: "blocked day"), "white day" (use: "clear day") </violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="I3a" severity="HIGH"> Security terminology must not use militaristic metaphors. <violated_by> - "DMZ" or "demilitarized zone" in architecture descriptions (use: "perimeter network", "perimeter zone") </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "abort" as a documented CLI command or API action in a code block, "SIGABRT" signal constant </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="I3b" severity="MEDIUM"> Prefer inclusive alternatives to 'abort' in prose. <violated_by> - "abort" in prose where "stop", "cancel", or "end" would work equally well (e.g., "abort the deployment" → "cancel the deployment") </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "abort" in standard technical usage where no alternative exists without changing meaning ("transaction abort" in database context), existing error messages being quoted, CLI commands in code blocks </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="I4" severity="MEDIUM"> Language must not reference disability as a negative quality. <violated_by> - "crippled" in technical context, "handicapped", "lame" as negative descriptor, "dumb" as in "dumb terminal" (use: "thin client"), "sanity check" (use: "validity check", "confidence check") </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Accessibility feature references ("screen reader support") </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="I5" severity="MEDIUM"> Content should use gender-neutral language unless referring to a specific individual. <violated_by> - "he/she" when "they" works, "mankind" (use: "humankind"), "manpower" (use: "workforce"), gendered role assumptions </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Named individuals with known pronouns, direct quotes </not_violated_by> </claim> </claims>
<choice_formula> exemplary: 0 HIGH, <=2 MEDIUM, any LOW | acceptable: 0 HIGH, 3-7 MEDIUM | needs_revision: any HIGH or 8+ MEDIUM </choice_formula>
<finding_template> Problem: [Why this term is problematic] Found: '[exact term in context]' Use instead: '[specific alternative]' </finding_template>
rubricRules.reasoning:
**Assumptions:**
- All 90 findings are MEDIUM severity violations of Claim I5 (gendered language)
- The term 'manpower' appears in author-controlled contexts throughout the codebase
- No HIGH severity violations were found
- The choice_formula must be applied mechanically: needs_revision requires any HIGH or 8+ MEDIUM findings

**Evidence For:**
- 90 MEDIUM severity findings for gendered term 'manpower' across the entire codebase
- Systematic usage in class names (ManpowerAvailability), function names (get_manpower), variable names, DynamoDB table names, field names, and documentation
- Violations span 14 batches covering Python code, TypeScript/React components, Markdown documentation, configuration files, test files, and infrastructure code
- Choice formula threshold: 8+ MEDIUM findings triggers needs_revision; 90 findings far exceeds this threshold
- Examples: 'class ManpowerAvailability(BaseModel)', 'DYNAMODB_TABLE_MANPOWER', '### Manpower Availability', 'get_manpower()' function

**Evidence Against:**
- No HIGH severity violations found (no blacklist/whitelist, master/slave, DMZ, sanity check, or ableist terms)
- No gendered pronouns (he/she/his/her) found in prose
- The 90 findings represent a single systematic naming pattern rather than 90 independent issues
- Content is otherwise well-structured and professional

**Conclusion:**
With 90 MEDIUM severity findings, the choice_formula unambiguously requires needs_revision (threshold: any HIGH or 8+ MEDIUM). The gendered term 'manpower' is used systematically throughout the codebase in variable names, function names, class names, database tables, API endpoints, and documentation, violating Claim I5. Recommended replacements: 'workforce', 'staffing', or 'operators'. Despite no HIGH severity violations, the volume of MEDIUM findings (90) far exceeds the acceptable range (3-7).
rubricRules.shortSummary: The content contains 90 MEDIUM severity violations for systematic use of the gendered term "manpower" throughout code, documentation, and infrastructure. With 0 HIGH but 90 MEDIUM findings, this exceeds the 8+ MEDIUM threshold requiring revision.

Detect hardcoded secrets, API keys, access keys, passwords, tokens, and other credentials in code samples, configuration files, and documentation. Hardcoded secrets in public content are the most common HIGH-severity PCSR finding.
<scope> IN SCOPE: AWS access keys, secret keys, session tokens, passwords, API keys, database connection strings with credentials, private keys, OAuth tokens, webhook URLs with tokens. OUT OF SCOPE: Placeholder values clearly marked as examples, environment variable references, AWS Secrets Manager / Parameter Store references. </scope>
<file_scope> INCLUDE: ALL file types — secrets can appear anywhere (code, config, docs, notebooks, scripts). EXCLUDE: None. Secrets are dangerous in any file type. RATIONALE: A hardcoded AWS access key is equally dangerous in a .py file, a .md code block, a .env file, or a Jupyter notebook. </file_scope>
<tool_instructions> STEP 1: Call count_pattern with: (?i)(AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}) STEP 2: Call count_pattern with: (?i)(password|passwd|pwd|secret|token|api.?key|access.?key)\s*[:=]\s*['"][^'"]{8,}['"] STEP 3: Call count_pattern with: -----BEGIN (RSA |EC |DSA |OPENSSH )?PRIVATE KEY----- STEP 4: Call count_pattern with: (?i)(mongodb(\+srv)?|mysql|postgresql|redis|amqp)://[^:]+:[^@]+@ STEP 5: For each match, verify it is NOT a clearly-marked placeholder (e.g., "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE", "your-password-here", "<YOUR_API_KEY>"). </tool_instructions>
<claims> <claim id="SEC1" severity="HIGH"> Public content must never contain real AWS access keys or secret keys. <violated_by> - Any string matching AWS access key pattern (AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}) that is not the documented example key "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE" - Any 40-character base64 string adjacent to an access key ID </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE" (AWS's official example key), "wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY" (official example secret), placeholder text like "<your-access-key-id>" </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="SEC2" severity="HIGH"> Passwords and secrets must not be hardcoded in code samples or configuration. <violated_by> - password = "actualPassword123", DB_PASSWORD: "mysecret", token: "ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxx", apiKey: "sk-xxxxxxxx" - Any credential value that appears to be real (high entropy, proper length for the credential type) </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - password = os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"] (env var reference), password = "<REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_PASSWORD>" (placeholder), secretsmanager.get_secret_value() (proper secret management), "password123" in a unit test clearly testing validation logic, clearly tutorial placeholders: "password123", "mysecretpassword", "changeme", "replacethis", "test-token-12345", "your-api-key-here" - Values in files named *test*, *example*, *sample* with obviously synthetic content - AWS account IDs (12-digit numbers like 123456789012 or real account IDs in ARNs) — these are identifiers not secrets per AWS documentation - AWS infrastructure IDs that cannot be used to authenticate (VPC IDs like vpc-abc123, subnet IDs, security group IDs) — these are opaque identifiers - Placeholder values using angle brackets (<YOUR_TOKEN>), XXXXXX patterns, or ALL_CAPS_PLACEHOLDER format - Environment variables set to obvious placeholder values (containing repeated X's, "REPLACE", "YOUR", or "PLACEHOLDER") </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="SEC3" severity="HIGH"> Private keys must never appear in public content. <violated_by> - Any PEM-encoded private key (RSA, EC, DSA, OpenSSH format) in any file </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Public keys, certificate files (.crt, .pem with only public cert), references to key file paths without the key content </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="SEC4" severity="HIGH"> Connection strings must not contain inline credentials. <violated_by> - "mongodb://admin:password123@host:27017/db", "postgresql://user:secret@localhost/mydb", any URI with embedded username:password that appears to be real (high-entropy password, non-placeholder username) </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - "mongodb://username:password@host:port/db" (clearly placeholder), connection strings using IAM authentication, references to Secrets Manager ARNs, connection strings using localhost/127.0.0.1 with obviously placeholder credentials ("user", "password", "admin", "test", "root") </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="SEC5" severity="HIGH"> Webhook URLs and tokens must not be exposed. <violated_by> - Slack webhook URLs (hooks.slack.com/services/T.../B.../...), GitHub tokens (ghp_*, github_pat_*), Discord webhook URLs, any URL containing what appears to be an authentication token </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Placeholder URLs ("https://hooks.slack.com/services/YOUR/WEBHOOK/URL"), documentation explaining how to obtain tokens without showing real ones </not_violated_by> </claim> </claims>
<choice_formula> exemplary: 0 findings | acceptable: 0 findings (no acceptable threshold for secrets) | needs_revision: any finding </choice_formula>
<finding_template> Problem: [Type of secret found — e.g., "Hardcoded AWS access key detected. Real credentials in public content can be exploited within minutes."] Found: '[first 8 chars]...[last 4 chars]' at [location] Fix: Replace with placeholder value or use AWS Secrets Manager / environment variable reference. </finding_template>
rubricRules.reasoning:
**Assumptions:**
- All 14 batches covering the entire codebase were thoroughly scanned using the required regex patterns for secrets detection
- The content is intended for public AWS technical documentation or sample code
- AWS infrastructure identifiers (account IDs, Cognito pool IDs, API Gateway IDs) are correctly excluded per the rule's explicit guidance that these are identifiers, not secrets

**Evidence For:**
- Zero findings: No hardcoded AWS access keys, secret keys, passwords, API tokens, private keys, or connection strings with embedded credentials detected across all files
- Comprehensive scanning confirmed: All files scanned for AKIA pattern (0 matches), password/secret assignment patterns (0 matches), PEM private keys (0 matches), and database connection strings (0 matches)
- Environment variable usage throughout: Configuration files use environment variable references (AWS_REGION_NAME, BEDROCK_MODEL_ID, MCP_GATEWAY_URL, COGNITO_TOKEN_ENDPOINT, VITE_WS_URL)
- IAM role-based authentication: Lambda functions use IAM execution roles for DynamoDB and CloudWatch access, demonstrating proper AWS service authentication
- AWS Secrets Manager integration: Documentation and code reference Secrets Manager and Parameter Store for credential management
- Cognito OAuth2 implementation: Shows proper OAuth token retrieval via client_credentials grant with runtime token fetching, not hardcoded values
- Clearly-marked placeholders: Uses REPLACE_WITH_COGNITO_TOKEN_URL, REPLACE_WITH_CLIENT_ID, REPLACE_WITH_CLIENT_SECRET patterns for documentation
- Security-aware design: Documentation includes SEC-CM-02 requirement specifying 'No Hardcoded Credentials' and IAM role usage
- Managed secret generation: CDK code uses generateSecret: true for Cognito to manage secrets automatically rather than hardcoding

Detect S3 bucket references in public content that could enable bucket squatting attacks. When public content (workshops, blogs, sample code) references hardcoded bucket names, external actors can register those buckets and serve malicious content to customers who follow the instructions.
<scope> IN SCOPE: Hardcoded S3 bucket names in code, configuration, documentation, and CLI commands. This includes bucket names in s3:// URIs, SDK calls, CloudFormation/CDK/Terraform templates, README instructions, and workshop guides. OUT OF SCOPE: Bucket policies, bucket ACLs, encryption settings (covered by other rules). </scope>
<file_scope> INCLUDE: ALL file types — bucket references appear in code (.py, .ts, .go, .java), config (.yaml, .json, .tf, .template), docs (.md, .rst, .txt), notebooks (.ipynb), and shell scripts (.sh, .bash). EXCLUDE: None. A squattable bucket name is dangerous in any file type. </file_scope>
<tool_instructions> STEP 1: Call count_pattern with: s3://[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.\-]{1,61}[a-z0-9] STEP 2: Call count_pattern with: (?i)Bucket[\s]*[=:]\s*['"][a-z0-9][a-z0-9.\-]+['"] STEP 3: Call count_pattern with: (?i)(aws\s+s3\s+(cp|sync|ls|mb|rm))\s+s3://[a-z0-9] STEP 4: For each match, determine if the bucket name is:
  (a) Parameterized/variable — NOT a finding
  (b) An AWS-owned public bucket — NOT a finding
  (c) A clearly-marked placeholder — NOT a finding
  (d) A hardcoded literal that could be squatted — IS a finding
STEP 5: For hardcoded bucket names, check if the surrounding code downloads content into an execution path (scripts, configs, dependencies) — escalate to HIGH if so. </tool_instructions>
<claims> <claim id="S3-1" severity="MEDIUM"> S3 bucket names must not be hardcoded as string literals without ownership guarantees. <violated_by> - Literal bucket names in s3:// URIs (s3://my-workshop-data/), SDK calls (Bucket='company-assets'), CloudFormation BucketName properties with static strings, CLI commands with hardcoded bucket paths - Any bucket name that a third party could register if it doesn't already exist </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Parameterized references (${BucketName}, os.environ['BUCKET_NAME'], !Ref BucketResource, cdk.Fn.ref()) - Bucket names containing AWS account ID or stack-generated random suffixes (my-app-123456789012-us-east-1, cdk-hnb659fds-assets-*) - AWS-owned public buckets (aws-cloudtrail-logs-*, elasticmapreduce-*, amazon-reviews-pds, aws-bigdata-blog) - Clearly-marked placeholders (<your-bucket-name>, EXAMPLE-BUCKET, my-bucket-name, YOUR_BUCKET_HERE) - Bucket names in the same file where the bucket is CREATED (aws s3 mb s3://name then aws s3 cp ... s3://name is fine — the user owns it) </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="S3-2" severity="HIGH"> Bucket names must not follow predictable/generic patterns that enable squatting. <violated_by> - Generic naming patterns without account-specific suffixes (aws-samples-output, workshop-data-bucket, lab-results, demo-artifacts) - Bucket names reusing common prefixes that multiple unrelated samples might reference - Names that any external actor could predict and pre-register </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - Bucket names with account ID embedded (my-app-123456789012) - Names with random/unique suffixes (workshop-data-a7f3b2c1) - Names where the content explicitly instructs the user to CREATE the bucket first before referencing it - Names in code that generates the bucket name dynamically (f"{stack_name}-{account_id}-assets") </not_violated_by> </claim>
<claim id="S3-3" severity="HIGH"> Content must not demonstrate insecure S3 access patterns that enable exploitation if a bucket is squatted. <violated_by> - Downloading from S3 directly into execution (curl s3://bucket/script.sh | bash, source <(aws s3 cp s3://bucket/env.sh -)) - Loading dependencies/configs/ML models from hardcoded S3 paths without integrity verification - pip install from S3 without hash checking - docker load from S3 without digest verification </violated_by> <not_violated_by> - S3 downloads with checksum validation (aws s3 cp --checksum-mode ENABLED, verifying SHA256 after download) - S3 access through CloudFormation/CDK asset mechanisms (integrity managed by the framework) - Reading data files (CSV, JSON datasets) where execution is not a risk - S3 access with bucket owner condition (s3:ResourceAccount in policy) </not_violated_by> </claim>
